name: Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve
problem: Interleaving prefill iterations with batched decode iterations raises the tail of time-per-output-token because a long prefill blocks every decode in the batch, capping achievable throughput at any latency target.
mechanism: Chunked prefill: split the prompt into near-equal-sized chunks and schedule those chunks with a chunk-level iteration budget alongside decodes, so no single iteration is monopolised by a long prefill. Adds stall-free scheduling, which admits new requests into a batch without pausing ongoing decodes, so large batch sizes raise throughput without paying the latency penalty. Uniform batches across chunked prefills reduce iteration imbalance, which minimises pipeline bubbles.
speedup_reported: Sarathi-Serve vs vLLM under tail-latency constraints, per the arXiv abstract: 2.6x higher serving capacity for Mistral-7B on a single A100 GPU; up to 3.7x higher serving capacity for Yi-34B on two A100 GPUs; and up to 5.6x end-to-end serving capacity gain for Falcon-180B when used with pipeline parallelism. Metric is serving capacity under a tail-latency constraint, not raw throughput. NOTE: this is the v3 abstract; the paper's own comparison table is against vLLM, and earlier versions compared against Orca as well.
notes:
Venue: the arXiv comment field is EMPTY, so anyone reading only arXiv metadata will call this a preprint. Venue is confirmed from the OSDI '24 program page. Adoption is the interesting part: chunked prefill is now the DEFAULT in vLLM and SGLang, so the mechanism ships — but the attribution is loose. vLLM's chunked prefill came from a separate in-house effort, not a code import; cite Sarathi-Serve as the paper that established the mechanism and the goodput metric, not as the source of the vLLM code.
